prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and trade shape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: B027 is the strongest candidate on the common criteria. It addresses a first-order question: who gains and loses when technology and trade change labour demand, and how persistent and geographically concentrated the adjustment is. The evidence is cumulative. It runs from the skill-demand and education-versus-technology work, through the task framework, to the local labour-market import-competition studies. It pairs new data and transparent identification with a conceptual frame, which is the combination I value most. It has been replicated, extended and contested for a decade or more, so maturity is not in doubt, and it has changed policy debate on displacement and adjustment. In my opening I ranked B017 first and B027 fourth, and I now put B027 first. The reasons are the broader evidence base, the cleaner maturity case, and a more defensible citation than B017 allows with its credited names. I also moved from Autor, Dorn and Hanson to Autor, Hanson and Katz. A citation covering both technology and trade needs the skills-and-technology anchor as well as the trade-shock anchor, and my opening trio covered only the trade-shock core.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the strongest reservation. The three-name cap forces a choice between Katz and Dorn. Dorn is a co-author of the central trade-shock papers, and Katz anchors a strand that is partly separate and also appears under B028. The task framework has other contributors who are not credited here, including Levy and Murnane. It also overlaps with work by a laureate recognised in 2024, and the 2023 labour prize is adjacent. The magnitude and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. The committee could reasonably view the technology and trade strands as two separate achievements, and a single citation may blur them.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the firm-heterogeneity trade candidate first. He rates misallocation (B017) lower because measured misallocation may reflect measurement error and adjustment frictions, and because Restuccia-Rogerson is a parallel contribution to Hsieh-Klenow. He also proposes only Autor and Hanson for B027, treating the Katz and Dorn contributions as separable.
responses.response: I accept the misallocation criticism and it moves my view. The size of the aggregate effect depends on firm-level measurement choices, and that is the main reason I no longer put B017 first. I disagree with dropping Restuccia. The 2008 and 2009 papers are close parallels, and the missing Rogerson in the credited names makes a clean B017 citation hard to write. On B027 I agree that the strands can be separated, but I would not shrink the prize to two names. The common object across the strands is how technology and trade shocks shift labour demand, and a two-person award would leave the skills-and-technology evidence without its anchor.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first. He warns that the task-based and trade-shock strands may be read as two separate prizes. He notes that the Katz-Murphy lineage complicates credit, that Levy and Murnane are not credited, and that the China-shock magnitudes face later critiques.
responses.response: I share the two-prizes concern and treat it as the main risk to the citation. I think a single citation holds if it is worded around labour demand and adjustment rather than around the task model. Wording it that way avoids claiming theoretical priority for the task framework, where the credited names do not cover the full lineage. The empirical object is the same across the strands: wages and employment responses of skill groups and local labour markets. I would not weaken the point about critiques of the China-shock magnitudes. I read those critiques as refining the persistence and heterogeneity results rather than overturning the core finding, which is why the citation says 'adjustment' and not a particular effect size.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B027 first with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He credits the local labour-market effects of import competition most cleanly to those three. He accepts that omitting Katz is a real attribution cost because the task framework has wider authorship.
responses.response: My opening trio was the same as his, and the argument for it is strong. The three ADH papers are the cleanest joint attribution on the list. I changed to Katz because the citation I propose covers technology as well as trade. Dorn's omission is a real cost, and I would not call the choice clear-cut. If the committee narrows the citation to import competition and local adjustment, Dorn should replace Katz. I treat the two trios as a choice about the scope of the citation, not as a disagreement about merit.

responses.point: Boppart ranks household debt and credit booms (B001) first. He argues that the 2022 prize covered banks and financial crises but not the household-debt channel, and that the results have been replicated across countries and episodes. He also notes some debate between the credit-supply and other explanations of the housing boom.
responses.response: The household-balance-sheet channel is distinct from the 2022 work on banks, and the pairing of Mian and Sufi is clean. This is why I keep B001 as an alternative and do not discard it. Two things keep it below B027 for me. The interpretive debate you mention is still open, and the evidence base is about a decade shorter than the labour-demand literature. I would not treat the 2022 overlap as disqualifying. The issue is whether the identification of the credit-supply channel has settled, and I do not think it has fully.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name depends on whether the citation covers technology and trade together or only the import-competition work.
How far later critiques of the China-shock magnitudes and long-run persistence change the weight of the trade strand.
Whether the overlap of the task framework with the 2024 and 2023 laureates' work reduces the marginal case for B027.
Whether the committee treats the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two.
Whether the household-debt evidence in B001 or the mobility measurement in B028 will be judged mature enough to rank above B027.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and institutional ties (Lund economic history, Lindvall, Cermeño and others) do not include any credited candidate on B027, B028 or B001. I have a general methodological affinity for new-data and archival work and an interest in technological change, and I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields.
